column6: Daniel’s Aramaic malkû names the enduring kingdom given to the humanlike figure; it is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k and appears in a scene where all peoples serve the ruler.

God names himself compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in covenant love; this is a close biblical pairing for the commentary’s Rahman/Rahim immediately before the title “owner of the Day.”
The same self-revelation says God forgives wrongdoing yet does not simply clear the guilty; this preserves both mercy and accountability in the sequence the commentary develops.
The proverb asks whether the one who weighs hearts will not know, then says he repays each according to work; it joins hidden motives to exact recompense in one passage.

column5: The Lord comes to judge the world
column6: The psalm says the Lord comes to judge earth and peoples with righteousness; creation’s response makes this a compact scene of universal judgment, not just a shared “day” word.
The next verse after Zephaniah’s approaching day names distress, darkness, and a trumpet blast; it adds the day’s sensory and cosmic disturbance to the commentary’s non-solar event.

WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 103:10. The psalm says God has not treated people according to their sins, a concrete counterweight to the commentary’s full repayment and merciful creditor.
Abraham’s vision shows a soul assessed by its deeds on a balance; this is a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary’s upright scale and final account.

column5: Prayer and offering for the dead
column6: Judas arranges atonement for fallen soldiers in hope that they may be freed from sin; this gives a different account of aid across death from the commentary’s claim that no one can pay another’s due.

column4: Unetanneh Tokef, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur liturgy
column5: Creatures pass before the King and records seal fate
column6: The prayer pictures all creatures passing before God, with life and death written and sealed; it extends the commentary’s sovereign day, personal account, and written verdict in a Jewish liturgical setting.

The kings and mighty see the Son of Man on the throne and are overcome with fear while the righteous stand before him; this adds the commentary’s royal sovereignty and the collapse of worldly rank to Enoch’s court scene.
Jesus says people will give account on the day of judgment for careless words; this gives a concrete relation between the commentary’s loss of speech-rights and the court’s accounting.

column5: The day’s date is not disclosed
column6: Jesus says no one knows the day or hour; alongside the commentary’s answer to “when?” by describing what happens rather than naming a date, it keeps the reader’s attention on the event and readiness.

Peter says all will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead; this gathers the commentary’s death scene, universal judgment, and personal accounting in a concise Christian formulation.

column5: Death and Hades release their dead
column6: The next verse after John’s opened books says sea, Death, and Hades give up the dead for judgment; it adds the gathering of every person from death’s custody to the commentary’s tribunal scene.
